title: Ephemeral degradation hunt and temporary isolation protocol (WIP)
content:
Status: WIP - aiming to capture a compact, repeatable hunt + temporary isolation protocol for short-duration GPU pool degradations that don't present as a full-blown outage ("silent drift").

Purpose and scope:
- Make it possible for first-oncall to quickly decide whether to: (A) temporarily isolate tenants, (B) enforce a quick autoscaler configuration change, or (C) open a deeper investigation.
- Target incidents: dedicated GPU pools where token throughput or p95 single-request latency drifts up by 10–40% for 5–30 minutes without obvious hardware failures or driver events.
- Not for: complete hardware failures, firmware panics, or sustained >30m degraded throughput that requires paging multiple teams.

Quick summary checklist (first 12 minutes):
1) Triage: confirm signal — check p95 latencies, request queue length, GPU utilization, alloc failures.
   - Grafana dashboards: pool-health (linked), allocator-telemetry, perf-traces.
2) Scope: which pool, which tenants (top 10 by qps last 15m).
3) Contain: if noisy tenant suspected, apply temporary isolation (soft-evict) to suspected slot ranges.
4) Stabilize autoscale: if autoscaler oscillation is suspected, switch to conservative policy and increase min-capacity by one slot.
5) Communicate: post an incident-thread in #sre and notify pool-owners channel.

Diagnostic signals to gather (commands, metrics):
- Allocator state: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SRE_TOKEN" https://allocator.redwood-internal/api/v1/pools/{POOL}/slots | jq '.'
- GPU telemetry summary: 
  - node-exporter metrics: nvidia_smi_utilization, gpu_memory_used_bytes per node (Grafana).
  - per-tenant qps and tail latency: query metrics: sum by (tenant) (rate(requests_total[5m])) and histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, tenant)).
- KV cache hit amplification: check cache-hit ratio and avg KV size. keyval_metric:cache_hit_ratio{pool="{POOL}"}
- Autoscaler events: kubectl -n allocator logs deploy/autoscaler --since=30m | grep -E "scale|hysteresis|policy"

Immediate containment options (choose one based on signals):
A) Soft isolation (preferred first step for noisy-tenant hypothesis):
   - Identify suspect tenants: top delta in qps or tail latency.
   - Run API soft-evict: POST /allocator/api/v1/pools/{POOL}/soft-evict with body {"tenant_ids": ["t-123","t-456"], "reason": "suspected noisy tenant - temporary isolation"}
   - Wait 90s for in-flight requests to drain; monitor p95 and allocation churn.
   - If metrics improve, keep eviction for 10–30m and create follow-up ticket for solutions-eng to throttle/shape.

B) Temporary autoscaler lock: (if autoscale flapping/incorrect hysteresis detected)
   - Patch autoscaler to ignore scale-down for 10m: kubectl patch deploy/autoscaler -n allocator --type=json -p '[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/metadata/annotations/sre-temp-lock","value":"true"}]'
   - Increase min replicas: kubectl scale deploy/autoscaler --replicas=$((current_min+1)) -n allocator
   - Rationale: prevents premature scale-down that causes repeated warmup and KV re-population which amplifies latency.

C) Emergency fallback routing: (if entire pool trending but other regions have spare capacity)
   - Flip routing policy for new requests to region-fallback for 5–20m: POST /router/api/v1/route-change {"from_pool":"{POOL}", "to_pool":"{POOL}-fallback", "percent": 100, "duration_minutes": 20}
   - Monitor backlog and SLOs across both pools.

Hypotheses matrix (what usually correlates with each signal):
- Noisy neighbor (single tenant spikes): high per-tenant qps, local GPU memory pressure, increased cache miss rate, increased allocator churn. Predicts immediate improvement after soft-evict.
- KV cache amplification during warmup: transient p95 spike after bulk-model load or version rollout; predicted improvement after cache-warm fill or if we pin a warmed model.
- Autoscaler misconfig (hysteresis too tight): repeated scale down/up cycles in autoscaler logs, sawtooth pattern in GPU utilization, worse tail latencies during warm windows. 
- Driver/firmware jitter: correlated node-level errors, dmesg/kernel logs, simultaneous p95 across many tenants but not per-tenant spikes. Requires infra-escalation.

Investigation playbook (deeper, if first containment didn't resolve):
1) Correlate with infra signals: check node kernel logs, GPU driver errors, and NVML warnings: ssh node && journalctl -u nvidia-driver -n 200.
2) Snapshot allocator decisions during the window: curl allocator trace API /trace?since=TIMESTAMP. Save to S3: s3 cp - s3://sre-artifacts/degradation-traces/{POOL}-{TIMESTAMP}.json
3) Reproduce load in staging: use the same request size and kv/cache seed to watch KV behavior.
4) If noisy tenant confirmed and tenant is internal/partner, coordinate rate-limits with solutions-eng + CS.

Operational notes and gotchas (lessons collected):
- Soft-evict is safer than hard-evict for warm caches; it preserves graceful shutdowns and typically avoids client errors.
- Autoscaler patching must be timeboxed; we add annotations to make rollbacks deterministic.
- Be careful with emergency routing: routing 100% to fallback increases cross-region egress and costs — warn finance/ops if >30m.
- When in doubt, prefer containment that preserves customer-facing SLOs over aggressive evictions which may cause request errors.

Post-incident followups (if isolation used):
- Owner: allocate to oncall who performed the action -> create JIRA SRE-2124 with: what we did, time-window, metrics snapshot, suspected root cause, next steps (throttle / quota / model-optimization).
- Run a 2-week experiment to detect recurring patterns: instrument a "quiet-drift" detector to alert earlier.
- Product/solutions engagement required if tenant is a heavy commercial customer: create a cross-functional ticket with CS and Solutions.

Open questions and TODOs:
- Add an automated soft-evict API that can be executed safely from the SRE runbook UI (current flow is manual API call).
- Is the temporary autoscaler lock safe for pools serving latency-sensitive customers at scale? Need performance test.
- Decide retention policy for allocator trace snapshots (currently ad-hoc).

Contact matrix and owners:
- Primary oncall (SRE): see rotation (PagerDuty) - Slack #sre-oncall
- Allocator eng lead: Priya Nair (priya@redwood-inference.com)
- Serving runtime lead: Aisha Patel (aisha@redwood-inference.com)
- Solutions/CS contact for heavy tenants: Rafael Gomez (rafael@redwood-inference.com)

Appendix: quick commands and snippets
- List top tenants by qps last 15m:
  curl -s "https://metrics.internal/api/v1/query?query=sum(rate(requests_total[15m])) by (tenant)" | jq '.' | head -n 40
- Soft evict example (curl):
  curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SRE_TOKEN' 
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' 
    -d '{"tenant_ids":["t-234"],"reason":"temp isolation for noisy neighbor hypothesis"}' 
    https://allocator.redwood-internal/api/v1/pools/dedicated-eu-west/soft-evict

- Revert autoscaler lock (remove annotation):
  kubectl patch deploy/autoscaler -n allocator --type=json -p '[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/template/metadata/annotations/sre-temp-lock"}]'

Notes-to-self: keep this doc intentionally compact. If we use soft-evict >3 times for the same tenant in a month, escalate to quota-based throttling.

End of WIP runbook. Please add experimental results and any additional safe commands that we can gate under a runbook-only RBAC role.
